extracted.intended_audience: scholars and advanced students of philosophy and literary criticism (readers of Schelling, Kant, and Coleridge)
extracted.subtask_description: Appendix of critical notes on Schelling's philosophical writings (with references to Kant, Boehme, Leibnitz, Berkeley, etc.), offering evaluative remarks about logic, clarity, sources, metaphysical claims, and explanatory power. The page consists of marginalia-style comments that recommend standards for argumentation and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preface with a canon of one's own logic
rubrics_metrics.description: "Would that he had prefixed to this work a canon of his own Logic, and, if he could, had taught us wherein his forms of thinking differ..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should state their logical/methodological canon up front and explain how their forms of thinking differ from established methods (so readers can follow novel procedures). A prefatory methodological statement helps readers judge arguments rather than guessing at implicit rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unexplained mystical allusions / Behmenisms
rubrics_metrics.description: "In truth from p. 429 I find little but Behmenisms, which a reader must have previously understood in order to understand"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on obscure mystical vocabulary or private allusions without explanation. Provide definitions, context, or quotations when drawing on idiosyncratic sources so general readers can follow the argument; unexplained allusions are an accessibility anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid circular or dogmatic assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated by the exchange: 'It must be so.' — 'Why?' — 'Because else my Theory would be false.' — 'Well! and what if it were?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments must not rest on circular claims that appeal to a theory's truth to prove premises. Avoid asserting necessities merely to preserve a theory; supply independent reasons or evidence instead of dogmatic 'it must be so' reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer explicit meanings to imperfect allegory
rubrics_metrics.description: "Light here means something: why not substitute that meaning?" and criticism of 'allegorizing ... so imperfectly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a term or image stands for a determinate concept (e.g., 'Light'), state that concept explicitly rather than relying on vague or half-formed allegory. Replace metaphors with clear propositions when the metaphor's intended meaning can be stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge sources and avoid obscuring dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: "How can I explain Schelling's strange silence respecting Jacob Boehme? The coincidence ... is too glaring to be solved by mere independent coincidence in thought..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When debts to earlier writers are evident, cite them or explain the relationship. Unacknowledged borrowing or silence about sources invites suspicion; transparency about influences strengthens intellectual honesty and contextual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accurate, concrete illustrations over vague mystical phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: 'Water is the great Nurse and Mediatrix of all growth ... This is better, as mere accurate, than Feuer und Wasser in Einem Grunde.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer scientifically or concretely accurate analogies when they illuminate a point. Vague or exotic phrasing that obscures empirical correspondence should be replaced by more precise images or explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep logical categories distinct (avoid category errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: "I find a confusion in Schelling of the visible with the conceivable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate different logical or ontological categories (e.g., the visible/sensible with the conceivable/intelligible). Maintain precision about whether a claim is empirical, conceptual, or metaphysical to avoid category mistakes that undermine argument clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand explanatory power, not mere conceivability
rubrics_metrics.description: "The whole hypothesis (for more it is not) will explain nothing, for this reason, that, putting it at the highest, it does but make an impression on our receptivity conceivable, but not that we behold a real object."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory hypothesis must do explanatory work — show how phenomena arise or are accounted for — not merely render them imaginable. Avoid theories that convert empirical intuitions into mere impressions without explaining objecthood or causal connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide full extracts/quotations where relevant and test hypotheses against the problem at hand
rubrics_metrics.description: "Why not have quoted all this from Boehme, as an extract raisonnS? But does the hypothesis ... explain the problem of evil?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on prior texts to support a theory, quote them sufficiently and assess whether invoking them actually resolves the central problem. Do not substitute partial citation or suggestive reference for genuine explanatory connection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish methods/means from objects/ends
rubrics_metrics.description: "The means, by which we arrive at the consciousness of an idea, are not the idea itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must distinguish between epistemic procedures (how we come to know) and the objects known; conflating method with the thing itself leads to category confusion. Make explicit what is evidence, what is inference, and what is the purported object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove possibility versus proving actuality; supply rigorous demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: "All that we want is to prove the possibility of Free-Will... Kant had unanswerably proved ... Time and Space are laws of the former only"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to distinguish providing a proof of logical/metaphysical possibility from proving actual existence. When a claim requires demonstration (e.g., possibility of free will), supply rigorous argumentation and avoid treating possibility as sufficient for reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overt contradictions, especially about Time and temporality
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection to 'It takes place out of all Time, and thence together with the first creation' — 'This has at least the appearance of a contradiction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that locutions about temporality (e.g., 'out of all Time' vs 'together with the first creation') are consistent and intelligible. Avoid claims that collapse into self-contradiction or which rest upon incompatible temporal predicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep theoretical claims consistent with practical certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: "In a word, the practical certainty is lost to us by reason of the theoretical, the theoretical through the practical; it is impossible that there should be at the same time Truth in our Knowledge, and Reality in our will."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorizing must not undercut the very practical certainties it purports to explain. Guard against theoretical moves that render moral or practical claims unintelligible; ensure theory and practice cohere to preserve normative intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reify abstractions or confuse antitheses with contraries
rubrics_metrics.description: "Schelling...commences by giving objectivity to abstractions. A acting he calls Will; the same Acted on, he calls Truth; and then... turns them into contrary things..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating abstract predicates as independently objective entities without justification. Be cautious about transforming relational or antithetical descriptions into substantive contraries; preserve the distinction between grammatical/metaphorical usage and ontological commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why representations must be referred to outward objects (necessity of reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is evident, that not only the possibility of a representation of outward things in us, but the necessity of the same, must be explained... why on this very account we are under the necessity of referring it to an outward object."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorists should account for both the possibility and the necessity (normative compulsion) by which mental representations are taken to refer to external objects. Provide an account of referential necessity, not merely of conceivability or habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat intuition/perception as involving active (free) elements when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: "In any case, therefore, the intuition must at least be considered as a free act, even though one that is occasioned by the impression."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing perception and intuition, clarify the roles of passive reception and active mental contribution; avoid reducing all intuition to mere passive impression. Specify when mental acts are explanatory or constitutive of objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not subject supersensual claims to sensory intuitions improperly
rubrics_metrics.description: "Surely this has too much the appearance of subjecting the Supersensual to the intuitions of the senses, and really looks like pushing in a thing merely to take it out again."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating supersensual/metaphysical claims as if they can be settled by ordinary sensory intuitions alone. Distinguish methodological domains and do not force metaphysical entities into sensory schemas where they do not fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise language and ensure editorial accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: 'Is there not some omission of the press here — that is fur den Besitz, — that we take the look cm/ on a future possession for the possession itself?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully edit and proofread to avoid omissions or typographical errors that can change sense. Precision in wording matters for argumentation; where the printed text seems faulty, note and correct or qualify the reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting vague general terms for concrete psychological description
rubrics_metrics.description: "For what is a motive but a determining thought? and what is a thought but the mind acting on itself in some one direction? All that we want is to prove the possibility of Free-Will... For what is a motive but a determining thought?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rest arguments on abstruse generalities (e.g., 'motive') without unpacking them into concrete psychological or conceptual operations. Explain terms by reference to observable distinctions or clear conceptual analysis rather than leave them as uninformative labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize sensation as at least minimally objective (do not treat it as purely subjective)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sensation, I assert, is not exclusively subjective, but of all the known syntheses of Subject + Object it is the least objective; but for that reason still objective — Sensation is Perception within the narrowest sphere."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When discussing perception theory, avoid collapsing sensation into mere subjectivity; acknowledge degrees of objectivity in sensation and situate it within a graded account of perception. Ground speculative claims in empirical observations where relevant.
